config.title: TanStack Query Basics

intro.title: TanStack Query Basics
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React application that fetches and displays a list of posts from a mock API. You'll learn the core concept of server-state management using TanStack Query, which simplifies data fetching, caching, and synchronization. The main technologies involved are React for the UI, JavaScript for logic, and TanStack Query's useQuery hook to handle API calls. By the end, you'll understand how to efficiently load and show data in your components without manual state management for loading and error states.
intro.usecase: TanStack Query is essential for building modern, data-driven web applications that require efficient server-state management. You'll use it in product dashboards to fetch and display real-time analytics, in e-commerce sites to load product listings and user carts, and in social media feeds to handle pagination and live updates. This pattern prevents manual loading states and refetching logic, letting you focus on building responsive UIs that feel instant to users.

objectives: Configure TanStack Query provider in a React application
Initialize a query client with default options
Implement useQuery hooks to fetch data from an API
Manipulate query states to handle loading, error, and success scenarios
Control query caching behavior by setting staleTime and cacheTime
Integrate TanStack Query with React components to display fetched data
Apply query invalidation to trigger data refetching

steps.title: Import React and TanStack Query dependencies
steps.instruction: Import React, useState from 'react', and the TanStack Query hooks and utilities you'll need: useQuery, useMutation, QueryClient, QueryClientProvider from '@tanstack/react-query'.
steps.hint: Use import statements at the top of your file. Remember to import both the hooks and the provider components.
steps.seedCode: // Import React, useState, and TanStack Query dependencies here
steps.expectedOutcome: The necessary imports for React and TanStack Query are added to the file.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react', and useQuery, useMutation, QueryClient, and QueryClientProvider are imported from '@tanstack/react-query'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've imported some dependencies, but check if you're missing any: React, useState, useQuery, useMutation, QueryClient, or QueryClientProvider.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are incorrect or incomplete. You need to import React and useState from 'react', and useQuery, useMutation, QueryClient, and QueryClientProvider from '@tanstack/react-query'.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns a JSX wrapper element (like a div).
steps.hint: Define the component using either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. Make sure it returns a JSX element.
steps.seedCode:
// Import React, useState, and TanStack Query dependencies here

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an App component that returns a JSX wrapper element.
successCriteria: The App component is defined and returns a JSX element (like a div).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main App component structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your App component returns a JSX element (like a div).
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component isn't properly defined yet. Create a functional component named App that returns JSX.

steps.title: Set up the QueryClient instance
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a QueryClient instance using the useQueryClient hook.
steps.hint: Call useQueryClient() and assign the result to a variable named queryClient.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: creating a hook instance
const queryClient = useQueryClient();
steps.expectedOutcome: The QueryClient instance is initialized inside the App component, ready to manage caching and state for TanStack Query.
successCriteria: A queryClient variable is declared and assigned the result of useQueryClient() inside the App component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling useQueryClient() and assigning it to a variable named queryClient inside the App component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The QueryClient instance wasn't properly set up. Remember to use the useQueryClient hook inside your App component.

steps.title: Wrap the app with QueryClientProvider
steps.instruction: In the return statement of your App component, wrap the existing content with the QueryClientProvider component, passing the queryClient instance as a prop.
steps.hint: The QueryClientProvider should be the outermost wrapper in your return statement. Remember to pass the queryClient variable you created as the 'client' prop.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component returns JSX wrapped in QueryClientProvider with the queryClient passed as a prop.
successCriteria: The return statement contains QueryClientProvider wrapping the content, with the client prop set to queryClient.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using QueryClientProvider as a wrapper and passing the queryClient as the 'client' prop.
steps.feedbackWrong: The QueryClientProvider wrapper is missing or incorrectly implemented. Check that you're wrapping the content and passing the queryClient instance correctly.

steps.title: Create a mock data fetching function
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create an async function named 'fetchPosts' that simulates fetching data from an API. The function should return a promise that resolves with an array of post objects after a 1-second delay.
steps.hint: Define an async function that uses setTimeout with Promise to simulate network delay. Return an array of objects with properties like id, title, and content.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an async function named 'fetchPosts' that returns a promise resolving to an array of post objects after a delay.
successCriteria: The App component contains an async function named 'fetchPosts' that returns a promise with setTimeout and resolves with an array of post objects.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is async, uses setTimeout with Promise, and returns an array of post objects.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't meet the requirements. Create an async function named 'fetchPosts' that returns a promise resolving with post data after a delay.

steps.title: Use the useQuery hook to fetch data
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, call the useQuery hook with a query key and your mock fetch function.
steps.hint: Call useQuery with an array for the query key (e.g., ['todos']) and your fetchTodos function as the queryFn.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useQuery hook is called with a query key and the fetch function, enabling data fetching in your component.
successCriteria: useQuery is called with a queryKey array and queryFn property set to fetchTodos.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling useQuery with both a queryKey and queryFn.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useQuery hook isn't properly implemented. Check that you're calling it with the correct parameters.

steps.title: Display loading state
steps.instruction: Inside your component, add a conditional statement to check if the query is loading and return a loading message.
steps.hint: The useQuery hook returns an object with an 'isLoading' property. You can use this to conditionally render content.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will show a loading message while data is being fetched.
successCriteria: The component contains a conditional statement that checks 'isLoading' and returns a loading message element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're checking the 'isLoading' property from useQuery and returning a JSX element with a loading message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loading state isn't properly implemented. Check that you're using the 'isLoading' property from useQuery and returning appropriate JSX when it's true.

steps.title: Display error state
steps.instruction: Add conditional rendering to show an error message when the useQuery hook returns an error.
steps.hint: The useQuery hook returns an 'error' property. Use a ternary operator or logical AND to conditionally render an error message.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will be able to display error messages when data fetching fails.
successCriteria: The useQuery hook destructures an 'error' property and conditionally renders an error message element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're destructuring the 'error' property from useQuery and conditionally rendering an error message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The error state isn't properly handled. Remember to destructure 'error' from useQuery and add conditional rendering for error messages.

steps.title: Display fetched data
steps.instruction: In the App component's return statement, add a <ul> element that maps over the data array to display each todo item in a <li> element. This should render after the loading and error states.
steps.hint: Use data.map() inside the <ul> to create a list item for each todo string. Remember to add a key prop to each <li>.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetched todo items will appear as a bulleted list when the data is successfully loaded.
successCriteria: The return statement includes a <ul> element that maps over the data array to render each todo item in a <li> with a key prop.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're mapping over the data array and returning <li> elements with a key prop inside the <ul>.
steps.feedbackWrong: The data isn't being displayed correctly. Check that you're using data.map() inside the return statement and that each list item has a key prop.

steps.title: Add a refetch button
steps.instruction: In your component, add a button that calls the refetch function from useQuery to manually trigger data fetching.
steps.hint: The useQuery hook returns a refetch function. Add a button with an onClick handler that calls this function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: button that triggers a refetch
<button onClick={() => refetch()}>Refresh Data</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button appears in the UI that, when clicked, triggers a fresh data fetch.
successCriteria: A button element with an onClick handler that calls the refetch function is added to the component's return statement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added a button with an onClick handler that calls the refetch function from useQuery.
steps.feedbackWrong: The refetch button is missing or not properly connected. Check that you've added a button with onClick={() => refetch()} in the component's return statement.
